topic: anthropic ai exploits linux kernel tcp flaw
headline_marked: [[Anthropic AI achieves Linux root access]] in 53 minutes via critical TCP flaw (CVSS 9.8)
headline: Anthropic AI achieves Linux root access in 53 minutes via critical TCP flaw (CVSS 9.8)
summary: A CVSS 9.8 vulnerability in Linux kernel TCP allows unauthenticated root access. Patches for Ubuntu and RHEL were unavailable as of October 30, affecting all kernel versions from 4.4 onward.
details: CVE-2026-98432, a CVSS 9.8 vulnerability, has been confirmed in Linux kernel TCP code. An unreleased Anthropic AI model demonstrated unauthenticated root access in 53 minutes. Ubuntu and RHEL patches remained unavailable as of October 30.

The core issue is a race condition during TCP connection establishment in IPv4. The kernel moves a pointer to IP options instead of copying data, leading to a use-after-free if another CPU core simultaneously handles a retransmitted SYN packet.

The kernel patch was written by Google's Eric Dumazet after a report from Anthropic's Xinyang Ge. The two-line change replaces `kfree()` with `kfree_rcu()`, delaying memory release until other CPUs finish reading the options under RCU.
This vulnerability affects all Linux kernel versions from 4.4, released in 2016, onward. Equivalent IPv6 code copies the options, so only IPv4 is affected.

On October 27, Anthropic published findings from using an unreleased internal research model to discover and demonstrate vulnerabilities in major software. The CVE-2026-98432 exploit was reported as one of five demonstrations, alongside attack chains targeting Chrome, Safari, Android, and Windows.

According to Anthropic, after an initial prompt, the Claude model independently built an exploit achieving unauthenticated command execution as root, without user interaction. This was demonstrated on a Linux server running an MPTCP (Multipath TCP) listener.

The exploit has two stages. The first bypasses KASLR by making the kernel read an attacker-controlled length field, revealing kernel memory layout in 48 minutes. The second uses the same use-after-free to overflow a buffer and overwrite a callback pointer, executing an attacker's shell command as root in another five minutes, totaling 53 minutes.

The race condition has a useful property for attackers: losing it causes only one handshake to fail, without crashing the system, allowing retries until success. Anthropic has not released the exploit code, tested kernel version, or test environment configuration.

Root-level remote code execution was demonstrated only on servers running an MPTCP listener. However, since Go 1.24, TCP listeners enable MPTCP by default when the kernel supports it, meaning many network services written in Go may implicitly use it.

topic: retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robot
headline_marked: [[Retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robot]], vows to do it again
headline: Retired professor arrested for blocking delivery robot, vows to do it again
summary: Carolyn Marvin, 78, was cited for disorderly conduct after repeatedly delaying Uber Eats robots in Philadelphia, sparking debate over human vs. machine rights on public sidewalks.
details: Carolyn Marvin, a 78-year-old retired University of Pennsylvania professor, was arrested on October 14th for repeatedly blocking an autonomous Uber Eats delivery robot in Philadelphia. This was not her first time, but it was the first time she faced arrest for delaying the robot's lunch delivery.

Marvin views her actions as a symbolic protest against the proliferation of delivery robots. She cites concerns about the displacement of low-income delivery workers, the physical hazard robots pose on sidewalks, and privacy issues from their embedded cameras.

She believes she has a First Amendment right to protest corporate abuses in public spaces, asserting that humans should have more rights than machines. Marvin compares her current mission to past civil rights and anti-war protests.

Her arrest occurred after she encountered a robot, stopped in front of it, and a crowd gathered. Police responded to a report of "criminal mischief" and issued multiple commands before handcuffing her and citing her for disorderly conduct.

Pennsylvania law, passed in 2020, classifies autonomous delivery robots as "personal delivery devices" and treats them as pedestrians. While vehicles must yield to them, these devices must yield to other pedestrians and pedalcyclists.

Despite the arrest, Marvin maintains her stance, stating she will continue to block robots if it's "convenient and possible." She believes her actions spark productive conversations and highlight important societal questions.
